title: Best Compression Socks (2026): 6 Picks and How to Choose the Right mmHg
summary: The best compression socks in 2026, compared by mmHg, sizing and materials, plus how to pick the right level for flying, long shifts, swelling and recovery.
body_markdown:
Two pairs of compression socks can look identical on a shelf and do completely different jobs. One is 8-15 mmHg and meant for a desk day. The other is 30-40 mmHg — a level used clinically for moderate to severe swelling and advanced chronic venous insufficiency — and is not something to buy on a whim.


That number, millimeters of mercury, is the spec that separates one pair from another. Below are six well-documented picks with their compression levels, sizes and materials, followed by how to choose the right level for flying, long shifts, swelling and recovery.


We didn't wear-test these socks. We chose them from manufacturers' published compression levels, sizing, and materials, favoring graduated socks that state an mmHg range on the label. Prices are for one pair, from each manufacturer's site unless noted, checked October 22, 2026.

## The best compression socks


### 1. Sigvaris Casual Cotton: Best everyday cotton pair


Sigvaris is a long-established compression maker, and its Casual Cotton calf sock delivers 15-20 mmHg in a Supima cotton knit with a flat toe seam and a knit-in top band designed not to pinch or slip. Sigvaris positions it for tired or aching legs, travel, jobs with long periods of sitting or standing, and pregnancy. ([product page](https://www.shopsigvaris.com/products/womens-casual-cotton-calf) )


**Good fit for:** Office days, flights, and anyone who wants a cotton sock that looks like a regular dress sock.


**Watch for:** Sizing runs A to C on Sigvaris's ankle-and-calf chart, so measure rather than going by shoe size.


### 2. Comrad Knee-High Compression Socks: Best value with wide-calf sizes


Comrad's knee-high sock is a graduated 15-20 mmHg design meant for all-day wear, sold in standard and wide-calf sizes. Comrad also makes 20-30 mmHg versions in recycled cotton for $42, with sizes up to XL and wide calf. ([product page](https://www.comradsocks.com/products/knee-high-compression-socks-varsity-2) )


**Good fit for:** Long shifts on your feet, and anyone who needs a wide-calf fit at the everyday compression level.


**Watch for:** The 20-30 mmHg versions are a step up, so treat those as a clinician-guided purchase.


### 3. Vim & Vigr Merino Wool Compression Socks: Best merino wool option


Vim & Vigr knits its graduated knee-high socks in 15-20 or 20-30 mmHg, with a merino wool blend that's latex-free. Cotton and nylon versions are also available, and every style comes in wide-calf sizes. ([product page](https://vimvigr.com/products/parisian-stripe-merino-wool-compression-socks) )


**Good fit for:** Travel and cooler months, when merino's temperature regulation helps, and people who want a latex-free sock.


**Watch for:** Sizes overlap (S/M, M/L, L/XL), so check Vim & Vigr's chart if you fall between them.


### 4. JOBST Relief Knee High: Best for a clinician-recommended level


JOBST Relief is a medical-grade circular-knit stocking from one of the best-known compression brands. It comes in three compression levels, open or closed toe, and in sizes from S to XL with full-calf and petite lengths. JOBST doesn't sell it directly; we checked the price at Vitality Medical, a medical supply retailer. ([product page](https://www.jobst-usa.com/products/venous-conditions/compression-for-everyday-use/jobst-relief) )


**Good fit for:** People whose clinician has specified a level, especially 20-30 or 30-40 mmHg, or who need full-calf or petite sizing.


**Watch for:** It looks and feels more like a medical stocking than a sports or fashion sock.


### 5. CEP The Run Compression Tall Socks 4.0: Best for running and recovery


CEP's tall running sock applies 20-30 mmHg in a thin synthetic knit built for training. It's aimed at runners who want compression during and after runs. ([product page](https://ceprunning.com/products/cep-the-run-compression-tall-socks-4-men) )


**Good fit for:** Runners and athletes interested in recovery; see the research on recovery below for what compression does and doesn't do.


**Watch for:** 20-30 mmHg is firmer than most everyday socks, so check with a clinician first if you have any of the conditions listed later in this guide.


### 6. Sigvaris Athletic Recovery Calf Sock: Easiest to pull on


Sigvaris's Athletic Recovery sock applies 15-20 mmHg with no compression in the heel and instep, which Sigvaris says makes it easier to put on and take off. It uses Drirelease yarn for moisture wicking and odor control, and comes in five sizes up to XXL. ([product page](https://www.shopsigvaris.com/products/womens-athletic-recovery-calf-sock) )


**Good fit for:** Walkers, post-workout wear, and anyone who struggles to get a snug compression sock over the heel.


**Watch for:** It's built for activity and recovery rather than dress wear.


## Compression levels: what mmHg actually means


The pressure a sock applies at the ankle is measured in millimeters of mercury, the same unit as blood pressure, and it is printed as a range because it varies with fit.


Clinically the categories are broad:[Cleveland Clinic](https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/treatments/23449-compression-therapy) groups compression therapy into low (under 20 mmHg), medium (20 to 30 mmHg) and high (over 30 mmHg), and a[CMAJ](https://doi.org/10.1503/cmaj.131281) review of graduated compression stockings uses the same split. Retail is more granular. Sigvaris, one of the larger compression manufacturers, sells these bands (the retail labels vary by seller):

Two takeaways. Most people shopping for travel or work are choosing between 8-15 and 15-20 mmHg, and either is fine to pick on your own judgment. And 20-30 mmHg is where this stops being a shopping decision:[Cleveland Clinic](https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/treatments/23449-compression-therapy) says stockings rated 20 mmHg or higher require a prescription, so at 20 mmHg and up, involve a clinician before you buy.


### Graduated vs uniform compression


Graduated compression means the pressure is highest at the ankle and eases going up the leg — the *CMAJ* review describes "the greatest degree of compression at the ankle, with the level of compression gradually decreasing up the garment," which is what helps blood move back toward the heart rather than pooling.


Uniform compression, the same squeeze the whole way up, is what many cheap athletic "compression" socks actually are. Not useless, but a different product, and not what you want if you are buying for swelling or a vein condition. The tell is the label: a graduated sock states an mmHg range. A missing number is itself an answer.


## Compression socks for flying


This is the best-evidenced use case in the category.


A 2021[Cochrane review](https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD004002_compression-stockings-preventing-deep-vein-thrombosis-dvt-airline-passengers) pooled 12 randomized trials covering 2,918 airline passengers, all on flights over five hours. Among the 2,637 participants with follow-up data in trials that put stockings on both legs, 50 developed a symptomless DVT: three were wearing stockings, 47 were not. The reviewers graded that as high-certainty evidence of a substantial reduction, and also found stockings significantly reduced leg swelling, graded low-certainty because trials measured swelling inconsistently. No significant adverse effects were reported.


One honest caveat: no deaths, pulmonary emboli or *symptomatic* DVTs occurred in either group, so the review could not assess those outcomes at all. A symptomless clot on a scan is not the same as a clot that makes you ill.


For a healthy traveler, 15-20 mmHg knee-highs are the usual starting point. If you have a personal or family history of clots, are pregnant, are recovering from surgery, or take hormone therapy, that is a conversation with your clinician before the flight rather than a purchase decision.


## Best compression socks for nurses and long shifts


On a 12-hour shift the problem is not clot risk. It is that your legs are visibly bigger at 7pm than they were at 7am.


That has been measured. In a 2004 study in[Dermatologic Surgery](https://journals.lww.com/dermatologicsurgery/abstract/2004/05000/compression_stockings_reduce_occupational_leg.18.aspx) , 12 volunteers had both lower legs measured in the morning and again seven hours later, wearing a different compression level on one leg at a time. Uncompressed legs gained an average of 62.4 mL on the left and 94.4 mL on the right. Light support stockings cut that to 40.3 mL, and the stronger classes reversed it, ending the day below the morning volume. The authors concluded that calf-length stockings between 11 and 21 mmHg "are able to reduce or totally prevent evening edema and may therefore be recommended for people with a profession connected with long periods of sitting or standing."


Twelve people is a small study, better read as a demonstration of mechanism than a definitive result, but it points the same way as a 2020 review in the[Porto Biomedical Journal](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7710214/) : prolonged standing is a risk factor for chronic venous disease, and compression stockings reduce occupational leg swelling.


So for nursing, teaching, retail, hospitality or warehouse work: 15-20 mmHg, knee-high, graduated. Three things matter more than the brand.


- **Put them on before the shift, not during it.** Compression prevents swelling, and it is much harder to pull a sock onto a leg that has already swollen.
- **Buy several pairs.** Elastic fatigues, and a stretched-out sock is just a sock.
- **Knee-high beats crew height** here, because it covers the calf, where the muscle pump does the work.


## Do compression socks help with swelling?


For everyday swelling, yes, with reasonably good support — and you do not need a strong sock to get it. The[CMAJ](https://doi.org/10.1503/cmaj.131281) review cites a meta-analysis finding that compression of 15-20 mmHg "showed beneficial effects on edema and symptoms, as compared with compression of less than 10 mm Hg or no compression." The Cochrane flight review found less swelling in the stockings group, and the occupational study above found the same across a working day. Three settings, same direction.


What socks do not do is treat a cause. Swelling that is new, in one leg only, painful, red or warm, or that comes with shortness of breath, is a reason to be assessed rather than to shop — it can signal a clot, a heart or kidney problem, or a medication side effect.


## Pregnancy, recovery and varicose veins


**Pregnancy.** Compression stockings are commonly suggested for pregnancy-related swelling and varicose veins, and they are low-risk. The trial evidence is thinner than their popularity implies: a[Cochrane review](https://www.cochranelibrary.com/cdsr/doi/10.1002/14651858.CD001066.pub3/full) of interventions for varicose veins and leg swelling in pregnancy included seven trials covering just 326 women, and the one small trial comparing compression against rest found no significant difference in lower-leg volume. Ask your obstetric provider what level they want you in.


**Running and training recovery.** A meta-analysis in the[British Journal of Sports Medicine](https://doi.org/10.1136/bjsports-2013-092456) pooled 12 studies and found compression garments had a moderate effect on delayed-onset muscle soreness and on recovery of strength and power, 24 to 72 hours after damaging exercise. That is recovery *after* exercise, not performance during it, and "moderate" is the honest word.


**Varicose veins and chronic venous insufficiency.**[Cleveland Clinic](https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/treatments/23449-compression-therapy) lists both among the conditions compression therapy is used for, alongside DVT, leg ulcers and orthostatic hypotension. These are diagnoses, not shopping categories, and the level should come from your clinician.


**After surgery or a clot.** This is where guidance has genuinely moved. Compression stockings were long prescribed routinely after a deep vein thrombosis to prevent post-thrombotic syndrome, but after[a large placebo-controlled trial](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736(13)61902-9) found no difference, current US guidelines suggest against routine use for that purpose. A trial of compression is still often reasonable for *symptom* relief in an acute DVT or established post-thrombotic syndrome — at a level and duration your clinician sets, not one you pick off a shelf.


## How to size compression socks


Sizing is the most common reason a pair fails, and it has nothing to do with shoe size.[Emory Vein Center's patient instructions](https://www.emoryhealthcare.org/-/media/Project/EH/Emory/ui/pdfs/vein-center/how-to-measure-for-compression-hose.pdf) for knee-high hose are straightforward: sit down, take your shoes off, put your foot flat on the floor, then measure ankle circumference just above the ankle bone, calf circumference at the fullest part of the calf, and calf length from the floor to the fibular head — the bony bump below the outside of your knee.


Match those three numbers to the manufacturer's chart rather than guessing small, medium or large. Three things follow:


- **Measure in the morning,** before your legs have swollen, so you size to the leg the sock is meant to hold.
- **A sock that rolls down at the top is too small,** not too long. A rolled band is a tourniquet at the widest point — the opposite of graduated compression.
- **Wide-calf sizing is a real category,** and sizing up a standard sock is not a substitute, because you lose the ankle pressure that makes it work.


The *CMAJ* review notes measurement "should be performed by a trained health care professional, often a nurse." At 20 mmHg and above, take that literally.


## When to talk to a clinician instead of self-prescribing


Compression is not neutral for every leg. The[CMAJ](https://doi.org/10.1503/cmaj.131281) review lists absolute contraindications to graduated compression stockings including suspected or proven peripheral arterial disease, severe peripheral neuropathy or sensory impairment, massive leg edema or pulmonary edema from heart failure, local skin conditions such as fragile skin, gangrene or severe cellulitis, and leg deformity preventing a proper fit. Its warning is blunt: "The use of graduated compression stockings on legs with impaired arterial flow can worsen ischemia."


Get medical advice before buying if you have:


- Diabetes, particularly with any numbness or reduced sensation in your feet
- Known or suspected peripheral artery disease, or leg pain on walking that eases at rest
- Peripheral neuropathy from any cause
- Heart failure or significant fluid overload
- Any open wound, ulcer, infection or skin breakdown on the leg
- New swelling in one leg, or swelling with pain, redness or warmth


The common thread: compression assumes you can feel a problem developing and that your arteries can push blood in against the squeeze. If either is compromised, a sock stops being a low-risk purchase.


**Paying with an HSA or FSA?** Compression socks aren't automatically a qualified medical expense under IRS rules. Our guide to[compression socks and HSA/FSA eligibility](https://www.withflex.com/blog/are-compression-socks-hsa-eligible) explains how the rules apply.
